Best Music Streamer for Plexamp and Navidrome | ComputingForGeeks

 If your music lives on your own server, the best network music streamer is the one that can reach that server without a phone in the middle. Plexamp, Navidrome and Jellyfin each talk a different protocol, and the three families of hardware people shortlist (WiiM, a Raspberry Pi with a HiFiBerry DAC, Bluesound’s NODE line) each speak a different subset of them. A music streamer for Plexamp that can’t see Navidrome is not a bad box, only the wrong box for that library.
 Original content from computingforgeeks.com - post 179664 
 We ranked six streamers by how each one plays from Plex, Navidrome and Jellyfin. Then we built the Raspberry Pi side for real (Plexamp headless, Navidrome’s jukebox, Squeezelite, a Jellyfin stream into mpv) on a lab VM with an ALSA card standing in for the DAC HAT. The WiiM and Bluesound picks come from maker spec pages and vendor docs, not our bench. If you’re still building the server half, our NAS picks for Plex and Jellyfin cover the storage. Prices and stock below were checked in October 2026.
 Quick picks: the best music streamer for Plexamp, Navidrome and Jellyfin
 Start from the server you already run, because that decides which protocol the streamer has to speak. Each pick below wins for a different library:
 Best overall: WiiM Pro Plus , about $220 to $250 (check the live price). Google Cast for Plexamp, Plex built into the WiiM Home app, DLNA and Squeezelite for the rest, plus an AKM DAC worth using.
 Best value: WiiM Pro . The same protocols and Ethernet port as the Pro Plus with a cheaper TI DAC, the right call if you feed an external DAC anyway. About $170.
 Best for Plexamp headless and Navidrome jukebox: Raspberry Pi 5 with a HiFiBerry DAC2 HD . The only option here that runs your server’s own player software. About $110 to $130 for the Pi plus about €99 for the DAC direct from HiFiBerry (check the live price).
 Best budget DIY: InnoMaker HiFi DAC HAT on a Pi 4 or Pi 3B+ you already own. About $30.
 Best for a hi-fi rack and an SMB music share: Bluesound NODE . Indexes up to 200,000 files straight off your NAS share, gigabit Ethernet, HDMI eARC. About $750.
 Cheapest way into BluOS: Bluesound NODE NANO . Same ESS DAC and gigabit port as the NODE, without HDMI. About $430.
 For most people running Plex or Jellyfin, we’d buy the WiiM Pro Plus and stop there. If your library is on Navidrome and you’d rather the music play from the server’s own queue, build the Pi. Bluesound only makes sense when you’ll point it at a plain SMB share and live inside the BluOS app, because it will not talk to any of the three servers directly.
 How we tested and picked
 The hands-on part is the Raspberry Pi stack, because that’s where the setup problems live and where no spec sheet helps you. We ran it on an Ubuntu 26.04 VM with two vCPUs and loaded the snd-dummy kernel module so the player software had an ALSA card to open, exactly the way a DAC HAT appears to Linux. Everything in the setup section further down is captured output from that box:
 Navidrome 0.64.2 with the jukebox enabled, driven over the Subsonic API until mpv held the ALSA device.
 Jellyfin 12.4.0 with a music library, streamed to mpv on the same card.
 Plexamp headless 4.13.2 on Node 22 (it crashed) and Node 20 (it reached the claim prompt).
 Squeezelite 2.0 from the Ubuntu archive, listing the card it would play to.
 We did not have the WiiM and Bluesound boxes on our bench. Their protocol support comes from the WiiM FAQ, the BluOS support center and each maker’s spec page. Every price comes from the live Amazon listing or the maker’s own store on the day we checked. A VM proves the software path, not sound quality, so we make no claims about how any DAC sounds beyond the maker’s published SNR. We left out the WiiM Mini, because it has no Ethernet port and no Squeezelite support, and the WiiM Ultra, because at about $349 it costs more than the Pro Plus for a touchscreen and phono input this use case does not need, and WiiM’s page says it does not support AirPlay 2.
 Compare Plexamp, Navidrome and Jellyfin support by streamer
 Use this table for the one question the box does not answer: how does each server’s music actually reach the streamer. Some routes let the streamer or its app talk to the server itself; for the rest, you need a phone app or a bridge in between.
 Streamer Plexamp / Plex Navidrome Jellyfin Wired Price band 
 WiiM Pro Plus Cast from Plexamp, AirPlay 2 from iOS, Plex in WiiM Home Symfonium casting; Squeezelite via Music Assistant Jellyfin DLNA plugin; Symfonium casting 10/100 About $220 to $250 
 WiiM Pro Same as Pro Plus Same as Pro Plus Same as Pro Plus 10/100 About $170 
 Pi 5 + DAC2 HD Plexamp headless (Plex Pass) Navidrome jukebox on the DAC; Squeezelite via Music Assistant jellyfin-mpv-shim, or mpv on the stream Gigabit About $110 to $130 + €99 
 Pi + InnoMaker HAT Plexamp headless (Plex Pass) Same as above Same as above Depends on the Pi About $30 + the Pi 
 Bluesound NODE AirPlay 2 from Plexamp on Apple devices only SMB share of the same files SMB share of the same files Gigabit About $750 
 Bluesound NODE NANO AirPlay 2 from Plexamp on Apple devices only SMB share of the same files SMB share of the same files Gigabit About $430 
 Read the Bluesound rows twice. BluOS support states plainly that BluOS does not support UPnP or DLNA , and its music services list has no Plex, Jellyfin or Subsonic entry. A NODE plays your library by indexing the folder over SMB, which works fine but ignores your server’s playlists, ratings and play counts. The WiiM rows are the opposite story: five different doors into the same box, so whichever server you run, at least one of them works without extra hardware.
 1. WiiM Pro Plus
 The WiiM Pro Plus wins because it accepts every route a self-hosted library can take to a box on a shelf. Plexamp on Android or iOS casts to it over Google Cast, and the WiiM Home app has Plex built in. Jellyfin reaches it through Jellyfin’s DLNA plugin (Home Music Share browses DLNA servers, or Jellyfin’s Play To pushes to the WiiM), and Squeezelite lets Music Assistant push Navidrome tracks to it.
 WiiM Pro Plus: AKM AK4493SEQ DAC, Google Cast, AirPlay 2, DLNA and Squeezelite. Image: WiiM. 
 Buy it if you want one box that plays Plex, Jellyfin and Navidrome without building anything, and you’ll use its own analog outputs into powered speakers or an amp. Skip it if your amp already has a good DAC, because the extra money over the Pro goes almost entirely into the AKM converter you’d bypass through the optical or coax output. The specs that matter, all from WiiM’s product page:
 DAC: AKM AK4493SEQ, 121 dB SNR on the line out, up to 192 kHz/24-bit.
 Outputs: RCA line out, optical, coax and a 12 V trigger; line and optical inputs.
 Network: 10/100 Ethernet plus dual-band Wi-Fi 5.
 Protocols: AirPlay 2, Google Cast, DLNA, Spotify Connect, TIDAL Connect and Roon Ready.
 The Plex integration is the part people miss. WiiM’s own FAQ says Plex is built into WiiM Home on every model except the Sub Pro and Vibelink, so the streamer pulls from your Plex server itself and your phone is only a remote. There’s no native Jellyfin or Subsonic client in the app yet; both are open feature requests on WiiM’s forum. Amazon listed it at $249 on the day we checked while WiiM’s own store showed $219, so compare both and check the live price before you order.
 2. WiiM Pro
 The WiiM Pro is the value pick because it keeps everything that decides compatibility (Ethernet, Google Cast, AirPlay 2, DLNA, Squeezelite, Plex in the app) and only cuts the DAC. If the digital output is going into an AV receiver or a standalone DAC, that cut costs you nothing.
 WiiM Pro: TI PCM5121 DAC, 10/100 Ethernet, optical and coax out. Image: WiiM. 
 Its TI PCM5121 converter is rated at 106 dB SNR, 15 dB behind the Pro Plus, and the analog input is sampled at a fixed 48 kHz/16-bit. Buy it to feed an external DAC or receiver over optical or coax. Skip it if you’ll plug the RCA outputs straight into powered speakers and care about the analog stage, since that’s exactly where the Pro Plus earns its premium. It ran about $170 on Amazon and on WiiM’s store, which makes it the cheapest box here with a wired port and every protocol in the table.
 3. Raspberry Pi 5 with HiFiBerry DAC2 HD
 A Pi with a DAC HAT wins anywhere you want the server’s own software playing to the speakers. It’s the only option in this guide that runs Plexamp headless, which turns the Pi into a Plex player you control from Plexamp on any phone, and the only one that can be Navidrome’s jukebox output.
 Raspberry Pi 5: BCM2712, gigabit Ethernet and the 40-pin header the DAC plugs into. Image: Raspberry Pi. 
 The HiFiBerry DAC2 HD is the converter we’d put on it. HiFiBerry rates it at 123 dB SNR with a 2.1 Vrms RCA output, and its shop page lists it as compatible with every Pi that has a 40-pin GPIO connector. The driver is already in the Raspberry Pi kernel, so setup is one dtoverlay=hifiberry-dacplushd line in /boot/firmware/config.txt plus disabling the onboard audio (remove dtparam=audio=on and add ,noaudio to the vc4-kms-v3d overlay line, per HiFiBerry’s guide). It is not sold on Amazon; HiFiBerry’s shop listed it at about €99 (check the live price).
 HiFiBerry DAC2 HD: Burr-Brown DAC, 123 dB SNR, 2.1 Vrms RCA out. Image: HiFiBerry. 
 Buy this pair if you run Plex Pass or Navidrome and you’re comfortable with a terminal. Skip it if everyone in the house needs a plain app with no setup: the lab section below shows the real failures we hit, none of which a WiiM owner ever sees. Also note that headless Plexamp is a Plex Pass feature on the Plexamp page , while casting from Plexamp to a WiiM is free.
 Pi prices are the moving part. Amazon had the 4 GB board at about $127 from a third-party seller, and authorised resellers were at $110 to $130 the same day, so check the live price before you assume the board is the cheap part. The 2 GB model is plenty for any one of these players (the heaviest, Plexamp, used 103 MB in our lab), but it was out of stock at both resellers we checked.
 4. InnoMaker HiFi DAC HAT
 The InnoMaker HAT is the budget route when you already have a Pi 4 or Pi 3B+ in a drawer. For about $30 you get a TI PCM5122 DAC, RCA and 3.5 mm outputs, and support in moOde, Volumio and piCorePlayer.
 InnoMaker HiFi DAC HAT: TI PCM5122, RCA plus 3.5 mm out. Image: InnoMaker. 
 Buy it to turn a spare Pi into a kitchen or office player for Plexamp headless or Squeezelite. Skip it for a Pi 5 build: InnoMaker’s own product page lists the Pi Zero, 3B, 3B+ and 4 but not the Pi 5, and only the Amazon title claims Pi 5 support. That conflict is enough reason to pair it with an older board and spend the extra on the HiFiBerry for a new Pi 5.
 5. Bluesound NODE
 The NODE wins when your library is a folder of FLAC files on a NAS and you want a polished hi-fi component that reads that folder directly. BluOS indexes SMB shares of up to 200,000 files, and the NODE adds gigabit Ethernet, HDMI eARC from the TV and a 6.3 mm headphone output.
 Bluesound NODE: ESS ES9039Q2M DAC, gigabit Ethernet, HDMI eARC. Image: Bluesound. 
 For this audience, the trade-off is big: BluOS has no UPnP or DLNA, no Google Cast in its spec, and no Plex, Jellyfin or Subsonic integration. Plexamp reaches it only over AirPlay 2 from Apple devices, and a Plexamp-to-BluOS request is still open on Bluesound’s community board. Buy it if you’ll point it at the same SMB share Navidrome or Jellyfin reads, and you want Roon Ready, Qobuz Connect and TIDAL Connect too. Skip it if your server’s playlists, smart mixes or play counts matter, because BluOS builds its own library and never sees them.
 Inside, it uses an ESS ES9039Q2M DAC with up to 192 kHz and DSD256 playback, plus RCA, optical, coax and USB audio outputs. Amazon listed it at about $750 with low stock when we checked, so check the live price and availability.
 6. Bluesound NODE NANO
 The NODE NANO gives you the same BluOS library model, the same ES9039Q2M DAC and the same gigabit port for about $430. It drops HDMI and runs from 5 V USB-C power, so it suits a desk or a second room rather than the TV rack.
 Bluesound NODE NANO: ES9039Q2M DAC, gigabit Ethernet, USB-C power. Image: Bluesound. 
 Every limitation of the NODE applies here unchanged, since both run the same BluOS. Buy it if you already own a Bluesound speaker and want the same app in another room. If you do not, a WiiM Pro Plus costs about half as much and plays from Plex natively and from Jellyfin or Navidrome through DLNA or Squeezelite.
 Set up a Raspberry Pi music streamer for Plexamp, Navidrome and Jellyfin
 Every block in this section was captured on the lab VM described above. On a real Pi the only difference is the card name: replace hw:Dummy with whatever aplay -l prints for your HAT (a HiFiBerry board shows as sndrpihifiberry ). Check the card first:
 aplay -l 
 You need the card name from this line for every player below, so note it down:
 **** List of PLAYBACK Hardware Devices ****
card 0: Dummy [Dummy], device 0: Dummy PCM [Dummy PCM]
 Subdevices: 8/8 
 Our first run of that command printed aplay: device_list:279: no soundcards found... even though the module had loaded. The user was not in the audio group, so it couldn’t open /dev/snd . HiFiBerry’s own setup docs warn about the same thing and give the durable fix, one command followed by a fresh login (in the lab we opened the device nodes for that session instead):
 sudo usermod -aG audio $USER 
 With the card visible, each server needs a different player. The three subsections below go in order of how much fighting each one took.
 Plexamp headless crashes on Node 22
 Plex publishes the current headless build in a small JSON file, so you can fetch the tarball without hardcoding a version. The archive is bzip2, which minimal images do not always ship. Our first tar xjf failed with bzip2: Cannot exec until we installed it:
 sudo apt install -y bzip2 curl jq 
mkdir -p ~/plexamp-dl && cd ~/plexamp-dl 
URL =$( curl -fsSL https://plexamp.plex.tv/headless/version.json | jq -r .updateUrl ) 
curl -fsSL -o plexamp.tar.bz2 " $URL " 
tar xjf plexamp.tar.bz2 
 That leaves a plexamp directory with the app and its native modules. Plexamp headless 4.13.2 ships a native audio module built for Node 20. On Ubuntu 26.04 the archive’s nodejs package is v22.22.1, and starting Plexamp with it dies before it prints anything useful:
 Error: Module did not self-register: '/home/user/plexamp-dl/plexamp/treble/linux-x64/treble.node'.
 at Module._extensions..node (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1864:18)
 at Module.load (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1441:32) 
 Whatever node --version prints on your Pi (Pi OS Lite has no Node at all), install the latest Node 20 build from nodejs.org into ~/node20 so Plexamp always gets the version it was built for. Node 20 reached end of life upstream in April 2026, so the nodejs.org build gets no more security fixes. Keep this player on your home LAN. The lab VM used the linux-x64 tarball; on a 64-bit Pi OS the commands below fetch linux-arm64 :
 mkdir -p ~/node20 && cd ~/node20 
V =$( curl -fsSL https://nodejs.org/dist/index.json | jq -r ' [.[]|select(.version|startswith("v20."))][0].version ') 
curl -fsSL https://nodejs.org/dist/ $V /node- $V -linux-arm64.tar.xz | tar xJ --strip-components=1 
 ~ /node20/bin/node --version 
 Then start Plexamp from the download directory with that binary instead of the system one:
 cd ~/plexamp-dl 
 ~ /node20/bin/node plexamp/js/index.js 
 On Node 20.20.2 it starts and waits for a claim token from your Plex account, using 103 MB of RAM while it waits:
 Starting Plexamp 4.13.2
Please visit https://plex.tv/claim and enter the claim token: 
 We stopped at that prompt, since claiming needs a Plex Pass account. After the claim, the Pi shows up as a player inside Plexamp on your phone, and you pick the DAC as its output device in that player’s settings. A cast target cannot match this, because the queue lives on the Pi and your phone can leave the house without the music stopping. Run in the foreground like this, it stops when your SSH session closes. The tarball ships a plexamp.service unit, but it hardcodes User=pi , /home/pi/plexamp and /usr/bin/node . Before you install it, change those to your user and to absolute paths for your Node 20 binary and js/index.js (systemd does not expand ~ in these settings). We did not run Plexamp as a service in the lab.
 Navidrome jukebox: “can’t connect to mpv’s socket”
 Navidrome’s jukebox mode plays tracks through mpv on the server’s own sound card, controlled from any Subsonic client that supports jukebox, so a Pi running Navidrome is both server and streamer. The steps below assume Navidrome’s .deb package, which creates the navidrome user, /etc/navidrome/navidrome.toml and the systemd unit. The lab VM fetched the linux_amd64 package; on 64-bit Pi OS the same commands fetch linux_arm64 :
 sudo apt install -y curl jq 
TAG =$( curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/navidrome/navidrome/releases/latest | jq -r .tag_name ) 
curl -fsSL -o /tmp/navidrome.deb " https://github.com/navidrome/navidrome/releases/download/ $TAG /navidrome_ ${ TAG # v } _linux_arm64.deb " 
sudo apt install -y /tmp/navidrome.deb 
 If you run Navidrome in Docker instead, none of the systemd steps below apply, and you pass /dev/snd into the container. For the package install, add mpv and put the navidrome service user in the audio group, because /dev/snd is readable only by root and that group:
 sudo apt install mpv 
sudo usermod -aG audio navidrome 
 The service picks up the new group at its next restart. Now name the card in navidrome.toml :
 sudo vim /etc/navidrome/navidrome.toml 
 This is the exact file the lab ran, with the dummy card as the default device. It replaced the packaged file; if you edit in place instead, keep the package’s DataFolder line and change MusicFolder to your library, which the navidrome user must be able to read:
 MusicFolder = " /srv/music " 
Jukebox . Enabled = true 
Jukebox . Default = " dummy " 
Jukebox . Devices = [[ " dummy ", " alsa/hw:Dummy " ]] 
 After sudo systemctl restart navidrome , the Subsonic jukeboxControl call with action=start failed with this, and the same error landed in the journal:
 { " status ":" failed "," error ": { " code ": 0 ," message ":" Internal Server Error: can't connect to mpv's socket: dial unix /tmp/mpv-ctrl-23ObdjWqAfyEyo0g1vJ9zu.socket: connect: connection refused " }} 
 Without the device lines, start returned "playing":true but mpv exited a second later and the next status read false , which is harder to spot. Running the same mpv command by hand as the navidrome user played fine, so file permissions weren’t the cause. The packaged systemd unit sets DevicePolicy=closed , which blocks the service from opening /dev/snd even when the group permissions allow it. Create a drop-in directory for the unit and open a new file in it:
 sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/navidrome.service.d 
sudo vim /etc/systemd/system/navidrome.service.d/alsa.conf 
 Two lines allow the ALSA device class and leave the rest of the sandbox in place:
 [ Service ] 
 DeviceAllow= char-alsa rw 
 Reload systemd and restart the service so the new device policy applies:
 sudo systemctl daemon-reload 
sudo systemctl restart navidrome 
 Repeating the jukebox calls after the restart held this time. Three seconds after the start call, the status shows the track playing at position 3:
 { " status ":" ok "," jukeboxStatus ": { " currentIndex ": 0 ," playing ": true ," gain ": 1 ," position ": 3 }} 
 ALSA agreed: /proc/asound/card0/pcm0p/sub0/status read state: RUNNING with the mpv process as owner, and that mpv was started by Navidrome with --audio-device=alsa/hw:Dummy . Navidrome itself sat at 43 MB of RAM and mpv at 68 MB while playing, which fits on any Pi you could buy today, and you can drive it from any Subsonic app on your phone that supports jukebox control. Log in as an admin account, because Jukebox.AdminOnly defaults to true. The first account you create in the web UI on port 4533 becomes that admin.
 Jellyfin stream returns 401 with api_key
 Jellyfin has no jukebox, so the Pi plays Jellyfin as a client: jellyfin-mpv-shim as a cast target, or plain mpv on a stream URL for a scripted player. The commands below need mpv , curl and jq , so install those first with sudo apt install -y mpv curl jq if you skipped the Navidrome steps. On our Jellyfin 12.4.0 server the lowercase api_key query parameter on the audio stream returned HTTP 401, and mpv refused to open it. We tested four ways to pass the same token to the same URL:
 api_key query: 401
ApiKey query: 200
Authorization hdr: 200
X-Emby-Token hdr: 401 
 On Jellyfin 12.4.0, api_key and X-Emby-Token were rejected, while ApiKey and the Authorization header worked. Use ApiKey or the Authorization: MediaBrowser Token="..." header in any script that builds stream URLs. The lab got a session token from the /Users/AuthenticateByName API and the track ID from a search; an API key created in the admin dashboard is the usual alternative for a long-lived player, though we did not test that path. Replace 10.0.1.50 , the user name, the password and the search term with your own:
 B = http://10.0.1.50:8096 
TOK =$( curl -s -X POST $B /Users/AuthenticateByName -H ' Content-Type: application/json ' -H ' Authorization: MediaBrowser Client="pi", Device="pi", DeviceId="pi1", Version="1.0" ' -d ' {"Username":"admin","Pw":"YOUR_PASSWORD"} ' | jq -r .AccessToken ) 
ID =$( curl -s " $B /Items?IncludeItemTypes=Audio&Recursive=true&SearchTerm=660 " -H " Authorization: MediaBrowser Token= \" $TOK \"" | jq -r ' .Items[0].Id ') 
 echo " $TOK $ID " 
 Paste those two values into the stream URL. With ApiKey , mpv played the FLAC track to the card at its source format:
 mpv --no-video --ytdl=no --audio-device=alsa/hw:Dummy " http://10.0.1.50:8096/Audio/ITEM_ID/universal?ApiKey=YOUR_TOKEN&Container=flac&AudioCodec=flac " 
 The AO line confirms 44.1 kHz 16-bit stereo reached ALSA with no resampling:
 ● Audio --aid=1 (flac 2ch 44100 Hz)
 Title: Sine 660 Hz
AO: [alsa] 44100Hz stereo 2ch s16
Exiting... (End of file) 
 Don’t run the Jellyfin server itself on a small Pi next to the player. It sat at 340 MB of RAM idle with a four-track library, which rules out a Pi Zero 2 W’s 512 MB once the OS takes its share. Run Jellyfin on the Jellyfin server you built for video and keep the Pi as a player only. If you buy a WiiM, note that Jellyfin’s DLNA plugin is in the default plugin catalog but is not installed by default, so install it from the dashboard first. With the plugin’s Play To feature, the WiiM shows up as a target inside Jellyfin; one WiiM forum user reports that route working while Jellyfin did not appear in Home Music Share, so try both before you blame the network.
 How much RAM a Pi streamer needs
 We measured resident memory for each player on the lab VM, because that number decides whether a 512 MB Pi Zero 2 W is enough. These are x86_64 figures and we did not measure arm64, so treat them as a guide rather than a guarantee:
 Process State when measured RSS 
 Squeezelite 2.0 Running, searching for an LMS server 41 MB 
 Navidrome 0.64.2 Library loaded, jukebox playing 43 MB 
 mpv (Navidrome jukebox) Playing FLAC to ALSA 68 MB 
 Plexamp headless 4.13.2 on Node 20 Waiting for the claim token 103 MB 
 Jellyfin 12.4.0 server Idle after a library scan 340 MB 
 Squeezelite or Navidrome with its jukebox fit a Zero 2 W with room to spare, but the Zero has no Ethernet and only 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, and Amazon’s only listing was a third-party listing at $85 for a $15 board. A 2 GB Pi 5 or any Pi 4 is the more sensible floor, and the microSD card you put in it matters more for a box that runs 24/7 than the RAM does.
 What to look for in a network music streamer
 Ignore DAC chip names until the protocol question is settled, because a great converter that can’t see your server is a paperweight with RCA jacks. Check these in order:
 Which server you run: Plex wants Google Cast, AirPlay 2 or a Plexamp headless player. Jellyfin wants DLNA or a cast target. Navidrome wants a Subsonic app that can cast, a jukebox, or a bridge such as Music Assistant.
 Who holds the queue: casting from a phone keeps the queue on the phone, while Plexamp headless, a Navidrome jukebox and WiiM’s built-in Plex keep it on the streamer or server.
 A wired port: lossless 24/192 over flaky Wi-Fi drops out first. Every pick here has Ethernet; the WiiM Mini and Pi Zero 2 W don’t.
 Analog or digital out: if an amp or receiver already has a DAC, pay for the digital output and skip the premium converter.
 Who maintains the software: HiFiBerry says its original HiFiBerryOS is no longer developed and the 64-bit successor is still in development, so a DIY build today runs on moOde, Volumio or plain Raspberry Pi OS.
 The TV side of the same library has its own guide to streaming devices for Jellyfin and Plex direct play . If you want Jellyfin and Navidrome sharing one small server, the ZimaBoard build runs both.
 Where each streamer falls short
 No pick here covers all three servers perfectly. Each one leaves a gap, and something else fills it:
 WiiM Pro Plus and Pro: no native Jellyfin or Navidrome client in WiiM Home, and only 10/100 Ethernet. Fill the gap with the Jellyfin DLNA plugin, Symfonium casting, or Music Assistant over Squeezelite.
 Raspberry Pi with a HAT: you are the support desk. Plexamp headless needs Node 20 and Plex Pass, and Navidrome’s jukebox needs a systemd drop-in before it can open the card.
 InnoMaker HAT: Pi 5 support is not on the maker’s own list, so keep it for a Pi 4 or older.
 Bluesound NODE and NODE NANO: no UPnP, no DLNA, no Plex or Jellyfin integration, and AirPlay 2 only from Apple devices. They play your files, not your server.
 If you only pick one, make it the WiiM Pro Plus for a Plex or Jellyfin house and a Pi 5 with the DAC2 HD for a Navidrome house. The Bluesound boxes are lovely hardware aimed at a different buyer, one whose library is a share, not a server.

 QNAP QTS vs Synology DSM for Music
 The QNAP QTS operating system offers Music Station as its built-in music app, which provides a web-based player with playlist management and album art. It is functional but not as polished as Synology Audio Station. QNAP also supports additional music packages through the App Center, though the selection is smaller than Synology’s Package Center.
 For users who want to install Minimserver for audiophile UPnP streaming, QNAP supports this through its app ecosystem. The ARM processor handles Minimserver without issues, making the TS-233 a viable budget option for high-resolution audio streaming.
 When to Choose This Over Synology
 The TS-233 makes sense if you specifically prefer the QNAP ecosystem or if you find it at a significant discount compared to the Synology DS223. The snapshot technology and Mac Time Machine support are genuine advantages. However, most music collectors will find better overall value in Synology’s similarly priced alternatives.
 With only 4 reviews at the time of our research, this is a newer product that has not yet built a substantial user base. The 4.2-star average is decent but based on limited data.

 The Asustor Drivestor 4 Gen 2 is the most affordable 4-bay NAS we tested, and it is specifically interesting for music collectors who need capacity and RAID protection without spending $600+. Four bays means you can run RAID 5, giving you three drives of usable storage with tolerance for one drive failure. That is significant peace of mind for a large music collection.
 I configured this NAS with four 8TB drives in RAID 5, yielding 24TB of protected storage. That is enough for roughly 12,000 FLAC albums. The 2.5GbE port delivered noticeably faster transfers than standard gigabit when copying my initial music library, averaging around 230 MB/s in our file transfer tests.
 The Btrfs file system is a standout feature at this price. Btrfs provides snapshot technology, data integrity checking, and protection against silent data corruption. For music files that may sit untouched for years, knowing the file system actively verifies data integrity is reassuring. If a bit flips on your drive, Btrfs can detect and repair it automatically.
 The Realtek RTD1619B quad-core processor running at 1.7GHz handles music streaming and file serving without issues. However, the 1GB of RAM is a constraint. Audio playback and basic file sharing work fine, but the NAS will struggle if you try running multiple apps or heavy music server software. This is a file server, not an app server.
 Tool-Free Installation and Setup
 Asustor designed the Drivestor 4 Gen 2 with tool-free drive trays, which means you slide drives in without needing a screwdriver. I installed four drives in under five minutes. The trays lock securely and the hot-swap capability means you can replace a failed drive without powering down the NAS.
 The Asustor ADM operating system provides a web-based interface for managing shares, users, and apps. The built-in music app, SoundsGood, offers basic playback and streaming functionality. It is not as feature-rich as Synology Audio Station, but it handles album art display, playlist creation, and multi-device streaming adequately.
 4K Media Streaming Beyond Music
 While this article focuses on music libraries, the Drivestor 4 Gen 2 also handles 4K video streaming to smart TVs and mobile devices. If you eventually want to expand from a music server to a full media server, this NAS provides the capacity and connectivity to support that growth without needing an upgrade.
 The 2.5GbE port ensures that even large video files stream without buffering. For music collectors who also maintain video libraries or photo archives, this NAS offers excellent versatility at a budget-friendly price point.

 Buying Guide: How to Choose the Best NAS for Music Libraries
 Choosing the right NAS for your music collection comes down to five key factors. I have broken down each one based on what actually matters when storing and streaming audio files, not generic NAS buying advice that ignores the specifics of music libraries.
 1. Storage Capacity and Bay Count
 Start by calculating how much storage your music library actually needs. A typical MP3 file is about 3-5MB, while a FLAC album averages 300-500MB. High-resolution DSD files can exceed 1GB per album. A 2TB drive holds roughly 50,000 MP3s or about 2,500 FLAC albums. Most home music collectors are well served by 4TB to 8TB of storage.
 Bay count determines your RAID options. A 1-bay NAS has no redundancy, meaning a drive failure loses everything. A 2-bay NAS supports RAID 1 mirroring, which duplicates your music across both drives. A 4-bay NAS supports RAID 5, which gives you more usable capacity while still tolerating a drive failure. For irreplaceable music collections, at least 2 bays with RAID 1 is the minimum I recommend.
 2. Processor and RAM
 Music streaming does not require massive processing power. An ARM quad-core processor handles file serving, DLNA streaming, and basic music apps without issues. Where you need an Intel processor and more RAM is when you want to run demanding music server software like Roon Core, Navidrome in Docker, or Plex Media Server with transcoding.
 If you are running a single music app and serving files to a few devices, 2GB of RAM is sufficient. If you plan to run multiple apps, Docker containers, or serve music to many simultaneous users, look for 8GB or more. The QNAP TS-453E-8G and UGREEN DXP4800 Plus are the standout options for heavy multitasking.
 3. Network Speed and Connectivity
 Standard gigabit ethernet (1GbE) delivers about 115 MB/s, which is plenty for streaming music. Audio files are small, and even high-resolution FLAC streams at a few megabits per second. Where network speed matters is when you are loading new music onto the NAS or backing up your library.
 A 2.5GbE port roughly doubles transfer speeds to about 280 MB/s. A 10GbE port, like on the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus, pushes transfers to 1250 MB/s. If you regularly add large batches of music, faster networking saves real time. For daily streaming, 1GbE is more than adequate.
 4. Music Server Software Compatibility
 The software ecosystem is where Synology pulls ahead for music use. Synology DSM includes Audio Station for built-in music playback and supports Docker for installing Navidrome, Roon, or Plexamp. The Package Center offers one-click installation of additional music tools.
 QNAP’s QTS offers Music Station and supports Minimserver, which audiophiles prefer for bit-perfect UPnP streaming. UGREEN and Asustor provide basic music apps but lack the depth of Synology and QNAP ecosystems. If music server software is your priority, Synology or QNAP are the clear choices.
 5. Noise Levels and Operating Environment
 If your NAS will live in a dedicated server closet or basement, noise does not matter. But if it sits in your listening room, bedroom, or living space, fan noise and drive vibration become real concerns. Manufacturers rarely disclose decibel ratings, which is frustrating.
 Based on our testing, the Synology DS225+ and UGREEN DH2300 were the quietest units. Look for NAS devices with variable-speed fans that spin down when idle, vibration-dampening drive mounts, and metal enclosures that dampen acoustic noise. Avoid placing a NAS directly on a wooden surface, which can amplify vibration. A rubber mat or foam pad underneath makes a noticeable difference.
 Frequently Asked Questions About NAS for Music Libraries
 What is the best NAS for music storage?
 The Synology DS225+ is our top pick for music storage. It offers 282 MB/s transfer speeds, Intel hardware transcoding, and Synology Audio Station for built-in music streaming. The DSM operating system supports Navidrome, Plexamp, and Roon via Docker. For budget buyers, the UGREEN DH2300 and Synology DS223 deliver excellent music streaming performance at lower price points.
 What is the music library on NAS?
 A music library on NAS is your collection of audio files stored on a network attached storage device instead of a local computer drive. The NAS shares these files over your home network using protocols like SMB, DLNA, and UPnP. This lets phones, computers, Sonos speakers, and streaming apps access your music from anywhere without needing the files stored locally on each device.
 Is 2TB a lot of storage for music?
 2TB holds approximately 50,000 MP3 files at 3-5MB each, or about 2,500 FLAC albums at 300-500MB each. For most casual music collectors, 2TB is plenty of space. However, audiophiles with large high-resolution collections may outgrow 2TB quickly. A single DSD album can exceed 1GB, meaning 2TB holds only about 2,000 DSD albums. Plan for growth by choosing a NAS that supports larger drives or additional bays.
 What protocols are supported by NAS?
 Most NAS devices support SMB (Server Message Block) for Windows and macOS file sharing, NFS for Linux environments, DLNA and UPnP for media streaming to TVs and audio devices, and WebDAV for remote file access. Synology and QNAP NAS units also support FTP, rsync, and iSCSI. For music streaming specifically, SMB and DLNA are the most commonly used protocols, with SMB preferred for Sonos integration.
 What is the best music streaming app for NAS?
 For audiophiles, Navidrome is the top free option, offering a Spotify-like web interface that works with any NAS supporting Docker. Plexamp delivers excellent mobile streaming through Plex Media Server. Roon is the premium choice for high-resolution audio with advanced metadata, but requires a paid subscription. Synology Audio Station is the best built-in option for Synology users. For Sonos integration, the native Sonos app with a NAS shared folder works seamlessly without additional software.
 Conclusion: Building Your Personal Music Server in 2026
 Finding the best NAS for music libraries comes down to matching your collection size and streaming needs to the right hardware. The Synology DS225+ remains our Editor’s Choice for its unbeatable combination of streaming performance, software ecosystem, and quiet operation. The Synology DS223 delivers the best value with the full DSM experience at a lower price. And the UGREEN DH2300 wins the budget category for beginners who want simple music storage.
 Whichever NAS you choose, pair it with quality NAS-rated drives like WD Red Plus or Seagate IronWolf, configure RAID for data protection, and set up automated backups before loading your music. Your collection represents years of curation and investment, and the right NAS keeps it safe, accessible, and streaming to every device in your home for years to come.

 Own Your Music: The Complete Self-Hosted Streaming Setup for 2026
 Bryan Moon · 
 April 21, 2026 
 · 
 self-hosted 
 music 
 plex 
 navidrome 
 jellyfin 
 streaming 
 homelab 
 docker 
 privacy 
 Spotify just raised prices again. Your "liked songs" playlist is buried under three new UI redesigns. And that album you saved last year? Gone — pulled by a licensing dispute you never heard about.
 This isn't a bug. It's the business model. You don't own anything on streaming services. You're renting access to a catalog that shrinks, shifts, and disappears based on contracts you'll never see.
 The alternative isn't buying CDs or dusting off an iPod (though you can). It's running your own music server — a Spotify replacement that lives on your hardware, streams to any device, and keeps your library intact for as long as you want.
 I've been self-hosting music for three years. My server holds 12,000 tracks, syncs to my phone, streams in my car via CarPlay, and costs nothing beyond the electricity to run a single container. This guide covers the complete stack: server setup, library management, streaming clients, and the workflow for actually discovering new music without an algorithm doing it for you.
 What You're Building
 ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐
│ Your Phone │◄────│ Plex Amp / │◄────│ Your Music │
│ (CarPlay) │ │ Navidrome │ │ Library │
├─────────────────┤ │ (Docker) │ │ (NAS/Local) │
│ Laptop │◄────├─────────────────┤ └─────────────────┘
├─────────────────┤ │ Reverse Proxy │ │
│ Work Desktop │◄────│ (SSL + Auth) │◄───────────┘
└─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘
 Three components:
 Music library stored locally (NAS, server drive, or external storage)
 Streaming server (Plex, Navidrome, or Jellyfin) to serve it
 Clients on every device for playback and offline sync
 Total time to set up: about an hour. Total cost: $0 if you already have a server.
 Step 1: Choose Your Streaming Server
 Three options dominate self-hosted music. Each has tradeoffs:
 Feature 
 Plex Amp 
 Navidrome 
 Jellyfin 
 Cost 
 Free (core), Plex Pass for offline/lyrics ($120 lifetime) 
 Completely free 
 Completely free

 Excellent (dedicated music app) 
 Good (web + Subsonic apps) 
 Good (Finamp on mobile)

 Offline sync 
 ✅ Plex Pass

 Resource usage 
 Medium 
 Very low (~50MB RAM) 
 Medium 
 Setup complexity 
 Low 
 Very low 
 Low

 ✅ Yes

 ❌ General media 
 My recommendation: Start with Navidrome if you want dead-simple and free. Upgrade to Plex Amp if you want the most polished experience and don't mind the one-time Plex Pass cost for offline downloads and lyrics. Use Jellyfin if you already run it for movies/TV and want one app for everything.
 This guide covers Navidrome (free, lightweight, straightforward) with notes on Plex Amp for those who want the premium experience.
 Step 2: Prepare Your Music Library
 Before you stream anything, you need music files. Here are your options:
 Sources
 CD ripping — The classic approach. Buy used CDs for $2-5, rip to FLAC with Exact Audio Copy (Windows) or XLD (Mac). You own the files forever. Storage cost: ~300-500MB per album in FLAC.
 Bandcamp — Many artists sell DRM-free downloads directly. Often available in FLAC, MP3 320, or WAV. The artist gets a better cut than streaming.
 Amazon Music purchases — Buying a physical CD or vinyl on Amazon often includes a free AutoRip digital copy in your Amazon Music library. These are DRM-free MP3s you can download.
 Beatport / JunoDownload — Electronic music-focused stores with high-quality downloads.
 Qobuz Store — Lossless downloads from a streaming service that also sells files outright.
 What About My Streaming Playlists?
 Services like TuneMyMusic or Soundiiz can export your Spotify/Apple Music playlists to CSV. This gives you a structured list of what to acquire — but not the files themselves. Consider it a migration checklist, not a direct transfer.
 File Organization
 Your streaming server expects a clean folder structure. The standard convention:
 /music
 /Artist Name
 /[Year] Album Name
 01 - Track Title.flac
 02 - Track Title.flac
 cover.jpg
 Tools like MusicBrainz Picard or Beets can automatically tag, rename, and organize messy downloads into this structure. Highly recommended if your library is a pile of files with names like Track_01(1).mp3 .
 Format Notes

 Variable, ~245kbps

 Good compromise 
 Rule of thumb: Keep FLAC masters on your server, let your client transcode for mobile if bandwidth matters. Navidrome and Plex both handle transcoding automatically.
 Step 3: Deploy Navidrome with Docker
 Navidrome is a lightweight Subsonic-compatible music server written in Go. It scans your library, serves a web UI, and exposes the Subsonic API — meaning any Subsonic client app can connect to it.
 Docker Compose
 # docker-compose.yml
services:
 navidrome:
 image: deluan/navidrome:latest
 container_name: navidrome
 restart: unless-stopped
 ports:
 - "4533:4533"
 volumes:
 - "./data:/data"
 - "/mnt/music:/music:ro"
 environment:
 ND_SCANSCHEDULE: "1h"
 ND_LOGLEVEL: "info"
 ND_BASEURL: ""
 Key details:
 /mnt/music:/music:ro — Mount your music library read-only. Adjust the host path to wherever your files live.
 ND_SCANSCHEDULE: 1h — Automatically scan for new music every hour.
 Port 4533 — Navidrome's default web UI.
 Deploy:
 docker compose up -d
 First run creates an admin user. Check logs for the auto-generated password:
 docker logs navidrome
 Log in at http://your-server:4533 , change the password immediately, and let the initial scan complete. For a few thousand tracks, this takes 5-15 minutes.
 Reverse Proxy (Optional but Recommended)
 If you want HTTPS and external access, put Navidrome behind your reverse proxy (Nginx Proxy Manager, Traefik, Caddy, etc.).
 Nginx Proxy Manager example: 
 Scheme: http 
 Forward hostname: navidrome 
 Forward port: 4533 
 Enable Block Common Exploits 
 Request a new SSL certificate
 For external streaming, you'll want this — it protects your login and lets you stream over HTTPS from anywhere.
 Step 4: Connect Your Clients
 Navidrome exposes the Subsonic API, so any Subsonic-compatible app works.

 Web UI : https://music.yourdomain.com — full-featured, no install needed
 Sublime Music (Linux): Native Subsonic client
 Sonixd (Windows/Mac/Linux): Modern desktop client
 Feishin (all platforms): Beautiful, feature-rich
 CarPlay / Android Auto
 Substreamer (iOS) and DSub (Android) both support in-car playback. The experience isn't quite as polished as Spotify's native app, but it's functional: browse albums, play playlists, and control playback through the car's interface.
 Step 5: The Plex Amp Alternative
 If you want the most polished self-hosted music experience — and don't mind a one-time cost — Plex Amp is the gold standard.
 Why Plex Amp?
 Native CarPlay/Android Auto — First-class in-car experience
 Offline downloads — Download albums/playlists for plane rides or dead zones
 Lyrics display — Real-time synced lyrics
 Automatic mixes — "Time Travel Mix," "Artist Mix," "Mood Mix" generated from your library
 Sonic analysis — "Behind the Lyrics"-style track info and recommendations
 Gorgeous UI — Album art, artist bios, "Popular Tracks" from your library
 The catch: offline downloads and lyrics require Plex Pass ($120 lifetime, or ~$5/month). Everything else is free.
 Setup
 # docker-compose.yml
services:
 plex:
 image: plexinc/pms-docker:latest
 container_name: plex
 restart: unless-stopped
 ports:
 - "32400:32400"
 environment:
 PLEX_CLAIM: "claim-TOKEN_HERE" # Get from https://plex.tv/claim
 TZ: "America/New_York"
 volumes:
 - "./config:/config"
 - "/mnt/music:/music:ro"
 Claim your server at plex.tv/claim , paste the token, and deploy. Add a Music library pointed at /music , let it scan, then install Plex Amp on your phone.
 Plex Pass Decision Tree
 Free tier : Stream your entire library, browse by artist/album/genre, basic playlists
 Plex Pass adds : Offline downloads, lyrics, loudness leveling, hardware transcoding, skip intros
 If you listen to music mostly at home on Wi-Fi, free is fine. If you commute, travel, or want the full premium experience, the lifetime pass pays for itself in under two years compared to Spotify.
 Step 6: Discovery Without Spotify's Algorithm
 The hardest part of leaving streaming isn't hosting — it's finding new music. Spotify's recommendation engine is genuinely good. Here's how to replicate it:
 Curated Sources
 RateYourMusic charts — Community-ranked best albums by year, genre, decade
 Album of the Year — Aggregated reviews from critics across publications
 r/letstalkmusic — Deep-dive discussions, weekly recommendation threads
 Spotify's "Discover Weekly" — Use it as a discovery tool, then buy what you like
 Bandcamp Daily — Editor-curated features, genre deep-dives, and emerging artists
 Build Your Own Algorithm
 Create a system:
 Discovery day (weekly): Spend 30 minutes on RateYourMusic, Bandcamp, or Spotify's free tier. Save interesting albums to a note.
 Acquisition : Buy 1-2 albums per week. Build your library intentionally.
 Listen : Actually listen to full albums. Not playlists. Not shuffled background noise.
 Log : Use Last.fm (still free!) to track scrobbles and find patterns in what you actually enjoy.
 After six months, you'll have a library that reflects your taste — not an algorithm's guess.
 Smart Playlists
 Both Navidrome and Plex support smart playlists:
 "Recently Added" — Auto-populated with new acquisitions
 "Never Played" — Rotate through your backlog
 "Top Rated" — Surface your 5-star tracks
 "By Decade/Genre" — Organized browsing
 These replace Spotify's "Daily Mix" with something more personal.
 Step 7: Backup Your Library
 You went through the effort of building this. Don't lose it.
 3-2-1 for music: 
 3 copies : Your active library + local backup + cloud backup
 2 media : Server/NAS + external drive or cloud
 1 offsite : Backblaze B2, Wasabi, or even a hard drive at a friend's house
 Tools:
 rsync for local sync: rsync -av /mnt/music /mnt/backup/music 
 rclone for cloud: rclone sync /mnt/music remote:bucket 
 BorgBackup for versioned, deduplicated backups
 Your music library is likely 100GB-1TB+. Cloud storage costs ~$6/TB/month. Budget for it.
 FAQ
 Is this legal? 
Yes, if you own the files. Rip your own CDs, buy from Bandcamp/Amazon, or download from artist-direct stores. The server itself is just software — what you put on it determines legality.
 How much storage do I need? 
Rule of thumb: ~300-500MB per album in FLAC, ~100MB in MP3 320. A 1,000-album library is roughly 300-500GB in FLAC.
 Can I share with family? 
Yes — Navidrome supports multiple users with their own playlists and play history. Plex does too, and Plex Pass extends sharing to outside your home network.
 What about podcasts/audiobooks? 
Navidrome is music-focused. For podcasts, use FreshRSS + a podcast client. For audiobooks, Audiobookshelf is purpose-built and excellent.
 Will this work without internet? 
LAN streaming works without internet. For external access, you need your reverse proxy or VPN (WireGuard, Tailscale) to be accessible.
 The Bottom Line
 Self-hosted music isn't about nostalgia or being anti-streaming. It's about ownership, quality, and intentionality. You decide what goes in your library. You decide how it's organized. You decide when something stays or goes.
 Spotify optimized for convenience. Self-hosting optimizes for control. Both are valid — but after three years of owning my music, I can't imagine going back to renting it.
 Start small. Pick one server (Navidrome), add one album, connect one client. Build from there. Your future self — the one listening to an album ten years from now that Spotify delisted in 2028 — will thank you.
 Questions? Find me in the Discord or drop a comment below. And if you found this useful, share it with someone who's complained about Spotify's UI lately.

NAS for Music Streaming: A Hi-Fi Setup Guide

 100W per channel at 8Ω

 Check price on Amazon → 
 A NAS for music streaming is a small network-attached storage box that holds your entire library on mirrored drives and serves it to every player in the house (Roon, UPnP, Plex, your phone) from one backed-up source of truth. For anyone with more than a few hundred albums, a two-bay NAS with two drives in a mirror is the right home for the music, and it costs about as much as a mid-tier streamer.
 It is also the part of a network rig that people most over-think. A NAS is a file server and nothing more, so a FLAC it serves is bit-identical to the same file on a USB stick, like the one in my drawer next to the remote that carries REW and my last session files. What the NAS buys you is one library, protected against a drive failure, available to everything at once. This is the box that holds the ripped CDs and hi-res purchases in my own setup, sitting quietly in a cupboard, doing nothing glamorous and doing it perfectly.
 Why a NAS beats a USB drive or a folder on your PC
 A folder on your streaming PC works until the PC is off, asleep, or busy. And a single drive works until it fails, which it eventually will. A NAS solves both. It is always on and low-power, so the library is reachable whenever you want to play, and a two-bay unit running a mirror keeps a second copy of every file so a dead drive is an inconvenience, not a catastrophe. It also decouples the library from any one player: switch from Plex to Roon, add a second endpoint, replace your laptop, and the music stays put.
 If you stream only from Qobuz or Tidal and own no files, you do not need a NAS at all, and I would not sell you one. But the moment you rip CDs or buy hi-res downloads, you need somewhere reliable for them to live, and a NAS is purpose-built for exactly that. It is the unglamorous backbone the whole network audio system rests on.
 Choosing the box: two-bay is the sweet spot
 For music, a two-bay NAS is almost always the right call. Two bays let you run one mirror (RAID 1), which means each drive holds a full copy of the library. Lose one, replace it, rebuild, and nothing is gone. A music library is small by NAS standards; even a large lossless collection with plenty of hi-res rarely troubles a pair of modern drives. Synology and QNAP are the mainstream choices with the friendliest software; Asustor and a DIY box are fine if you enjoy the tinkering. Buy for quiet operation and easy software, not for raw horsepower. Serving FLAC is a light job.
 Four-bay units make sense only if you are also storing video, photos and backups for the whole household, or you want a more resilient RAID level. For audio alone, two bays and a mirror is the unfussy answer that I would point almost every reader toward. Pick the box around the software you will actually use day to day.
 Drives and RAID without the jargon
 Use NAS-rated drives, the ones built for always-on duty like WD Red or Seagate IronWolf, rather than cheap desktop drives, because a NAS spins them around the clock. Two identical drives in a mirror is all the redundancy a music library needs. Size them generously: work out your current library size, double it for headroom, and buy that. Lossless audio is modest. A big collection still fits comfortably on a pair of mainstream-capacity NAS drives with room to grow for years.
 One thing a mirror is not : a backup. RAID protects against a drive dying; it does not protect against accidental deletion, ransomware, or the house flooding. Keep a separate backup of the library, either an external drive you rotate offsite or a cloud copy, so a mistake or a disaster never costs you the collection. I learned that on a far smaller file: my mic calibration file is saved in two places now because I lost it once. The 3-2-1 idea (three copies, two media, one offsite) is worth following for music you have spent years ripping and curating.
 Choice Music-only pick Why 
 Bays Two-bay Allows a mirror; music libraries are small 
 RAID RAID 1 (mirror) Full second copy; simple to rebuild 
 Drives NAS-rated, identical pair Built for 24/7 duty; matched for the mirror 
 Network Wired gigabit Reliable serving; trivial bandwidth for audio 
 Backup Separate copy, offsite RAID is not a backup 
 How the NAS actually serves your music
 A NAS speaks several languages at once. It can share files over SMB so a Roon Core or a PC player sees the library as a network folder. It can run a built-in UPnP/DLNA media server so any UPnP-aware streamer finds the music directly. Synology and QNAP can even host a Roon Core or Plex Media Server on the NAS itself if the model is a 64-bit Intel/AMD (x86) unit, though I prefer to keep Roon on a separate NUC and let the NAS just hold the files. Pick the method that matches your software; all of them deliver the same bit-perfect data.
 The structure of the library matters more than people expect. Not for sound. For sanity. Keep a clean folder tree (Artist / Album / tracks) and tag the files consistently before you point Roon or Plex at it. Good tags in means a tidy, searchable library out; messy tags mean a frustrating one no software can fully rescue. Get the organisation right once and every player you ever use inherits it.
 Power, noise, and where to put a music NAS
 A two-bay NAS is a low-key houseguest. Most draw little power at idle and spin the drives down when nothing is reading them, so leaving it on around the clock costs about $17 a year (12 W average at $0.16/kWh), not a scary power bill. The noise is mostly the drives, not the fan. A pair of NAS-rated mechanical drives makes a soft, occasional chatter under load and is near-silent at idle. If even that bothers you, solid-state drives eliminate it entirely at a higher price per terabyte, which only makes sense for a small library.
 Placement is easy because the NAS does not need to live near the hi-fi — it talks to your players over the network, so a cupboard, an office or a utility room is ideal. Put it somewhere ventilated, out of direct sun and away from the dustiest corner of the house, give it a wired connection, and forget about it. Mine is out of earshot behind a closed cupboard door, which is exactly where a file server belongs.
 Networking the NAS
 Wire the NAS to your router or switch with Ethernet. Audio needs almost no bandwidth. Even a stack of simultaneous hi-res streams is a rounding error on a gigabit link, so the wired connection is about reliability and the NAS being reachable, not speed. Keep it on the same network as your players, give it a fixed address so your software always finds it, and you are done. None of this changes the sound; it changes whether the music plays without hiccups, which is what the network layer is responsible for.
 Treat the storage the way you treat the network. Judge it on whether it stays up, then leave it alone. What you actually hear gets decided further down the chain.
 As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. A starter setup is two boxes of shopping: a two-bay NAS and a matched pair of NAS-rated hard drives to run in a mirror.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Does a NAS improve music sound quality?
 No. A NAS is a file server, and a FLAC it serves is bit-identical to the same file anywhere else. It improves organisation, reliability and reach, not sound. Sound quality is decided downstream by the DAC, amp, speakers and room.
 How big a NAS do I need for a music library?
 Smaller than you think. Lossless audio is modest, so a large collection with plenty of hi-res fits comfortably on a pair of mainstream-capacity NAS drives. Size your current library, double it for headroom, and buy that.
 Do I need RAID for a music NAS?
 A two-bay mirror (RAID 1) is worth it: each drive holds a full copy, so a failed drive does not lose data. But RAID is not a backup. Keep a separate, offsite copy to protect against deletion or disaster.
 Can a NAS run Roon or Plex directly?
 Yes, if the model is powerful enough. Synology and QNAP can host a Roon Core (64-bit Intel/AMD models only) or Plex Media Server. Many people, including me, prefer to keep Roon on a separate low-power computer and let the NAS simply store and serve the files.
 Should the NAS be wired or wireless?
 Wired. Audio needs almost no bandwidth, so Ethernet is about reliability and keeping the NAS reachable, not speed. Give it a fixed address on the same network as your players so your software always finds it.

 Why 
 Best overall

 Best for federation/social

 Best library organizer (not a server)

 What to Look for in a Self-Hosted Music Server
 Before picking a server, know what actually matters:
 Subsonic API compatibility. This is the single most important factor for mobile listening. The Subsonic API is a de facto standard that dozens of mobile apps support — Symfonium (Android), play:Sub (iOS), DSub, Ultrasonic, and more. If a server speaks Subsonic, you get excellent mobile apps for free without the project maintaining its own. Navidrome, Ampache, gonic, and Airsonic-Advanced all support it.
 Transcoding. If your library is FLAC and you want to stream over cellular, the server needs to transcode to a lower bitrate on the fly. Most servers handle this, but check whether it needs FFmpeg installed separately.
 Resource usage. Music servers vary wildly. Navidrome and gonic run comfortably on a Raspberry Pi. Funkwhale and Jellyfin need a real server with 2-4 GB of RAM. Match the server to your hardware.
 Multi-user support. If your household shares a server, you want separate accounts with independent playlists, favorites, and play history. Every server on this list supports multiple users, but the quality of the implementation varies.
 Smart playlists. Auto-generated playlists based on rules (genre, year, play count, rating) are what separate a music server from a file browser. Navidrome, Ampache, and Koel do this well. Gonic does not.
 The Full Ranking
 1. Navidrome -- Best Overall
 Navidrome is the best self-hosted music streaming server for most people. It is lightweight (30-50 MB of RAM idle), fast (written in Go), and fully compatible with the Subsonic API. That API compatibility means you can use any Subsonic-compatible mobile app — Symfonium, play:Sub, DSub, Ultrasonic — as your client. The built-in web UI is clean and responsive, with album art, smart playlists, lyrics, and Last.fm scrobbling.
 Navidrome scans your existing music directory without modifying or copying files. Point it at your /music folder and it indexes everything. It supports FLAC, MP3, AAC, OGG, OPUS, WMA, and more. Transcoding is handled via FFmpeg when clients request a lower bitrate.
 The project is actively maintained with frequent releases. It went from v0.54 to v0.60.3 in early 2026, adding Jukebox mode, improved smart playlists, and better multi-disk album handling.
 Pros: 
 Extremely lightweight — runs on a Raspberry Pi with room to spare
 Full Subsonic API means dozens of mobile app choices
 Clean web UI with smart playlists, favorites, ratings, and lyrics
 Fast library scanning even with 100,000+ tracks
 Last.fm and ListenBrainz scrobbling built in
 Multi-user with per-user playlists and play history
 Single Go binary or Docker image — trivial to deploy
 Cons: 
 No podcast support (it is a music server, not a podcast player)
 No video support (use Jellyfin for that)
 No federation or social features
 Web UI is functional but not as visually rich as Koel
 Best for: Anyone who wants a dedicated music server that is fast, light, and works with the best mobile apps available.
 Read our full guide: How to Self-Host Navidrome 
 Quick Start: Navidrome with Docker Compose
 services : 
 navidrome : 
 image : deluan/navidrome:0.60.3 
 container_name : navidrome 
 restart : unless-stopped 
 ports : 
 - " 4533:4533" # Web UI and Subsonic API 
 environment : 
 ND_SCANSCHEDULE : " 1h" # Rescan library every hour 
 ND_LOGLEVEL : " info" 
 ND_BASEURL : " " # Set to "/navidrome" if behind a subpath proxy 
 ND_SESSIONTIMEOUT : " 24h" 
 ND_ENABLETRANSCODINGCONFIG : " true" # Allow users to configure transcoding 
 volumes : 
 - navidrome-data:/data # Database and cache 
 - /path/to/your/music:/music:ro # CHANGE: Your music library (read-only) 
 volumes : 
 navidrome-data : 
 Start it with docker compose up -d and open http://your-server:4533 . Create your admin account on first access. Connect a mobile app using the server URL with /rest as the Subsonic endpoint.
 2. Funkwhale -- Best for Social and Federation
 Funkwhale is not just a music server — it is a federated music platform. It supports ActivityPub, the same protocol behind Mastodon, meaning Funkwhale instances can share music libraries with each other. Upload your own music, subscribe to podcasts, follow users on other instances, and build shared playlists across the fediverse.
 Funkwhale has a modern web UI with playlist management, favorites, radio modes, and podcast support. It uses a Django/Python backend with PostgreSQL and Redis, which means it is heavier than Navidrome — expect 500 MB to 1 GB of RAM usage.
 Pros: 
 ActivityPub federation — share and discover music across instances
 Podcast support built in
 Modern, attractive web UI
 Channels system for content organization
 Multi-user with granular permissions
 API for third-party clients
 Cons: 
 Significantly heavier than Navidrome (PostgreSQL + Redis + Celery workers)
 No Subsonic API — limited mobile app options (Funkwhale has its own app, but ecosystem is small)
 Federation features require a publicly accessible server with a domain
 Setup is more involved than simpler servers
 Smaller community and slower release cadence
 Best for: Users who want social features, federation with other instances, and podcast support alongside their music library.
 Read our full guide: How to Self-Host Funkwhale 
 3. Jellyfin -- Best All-in-One Media Server
 Jellyfin is primarily a video media server, but its music support is solid enough to be a strong contender — especially if you already run it for movies and TV. You get a unified library for video, music, audiobooks, and photos, with a single web UI and mobile apps covering everything.
 Jellyfin's music features include album browsing, artist pages, playlists, lyrics, and Last.fm scrobbling via plugin. It supports hardware transcoding for video (Intel QSV, NVIDIA NVENC, VA-API), and software transcoding for audio. The mobile apps (Jellyfin for Android/iOS, Finamp for music-focused use) are free.
 The trade-off is that Jellyfin's music experience is a generalist's implementation. It lacks Subsonic API support (unless you add a plugin), smart playlists are limited compared to Navidrome, and the music UI is not as refined as a dedicated music server.
 Pros: 
 One server for all your media — video, music, books, photos
 Completely free and open-source, no premium tier
 Hardware transcoding at no cost
 Finamp mobile app is a good dedicated music client
 Active development and large community
 Plugin ecosystem (Last.fm, Lyrics, OpenSubtitles)
 Cons: 
 Music is not the primary focus — UI is video-oriented
 No native Subsonic API (plugin exists but is unofficial)
 Smart playlist support is basic
 Heavier than dedicated music servers (1-2 GB RAM minimum)
 Library scanning can be slower with large music collections
 Best for: Users who already run Jellyfin for video and want one server for everything, or who want a single-install solution for all media types.
 Read our full guide: How to Self-Host Jellyfin 
 4. Koel -- Best Web UI
 Koel has the most visually polished web interface of any self-hosted music server. Built with Vue.js, it looks and feels like a modern streaming service — album art grids, smooth transitions, a built-in equalizer, and a visualizer. If you primarily listen to music from a browser and want the experience to feel like Spotify, Koel delivers.
 Koel supports smart playlists, Last.fm scrobbling, optional Spotify integration (for browsing Spotify's catalog alongside your local library), and multi-user accounts. It is a Laravel/PHP application backed by MariaDB.
 Pros: 
 The best-looking web UI of any self-hosted music server
 Built-in equalizer and visualizer
 Smart playlists with rule-based filtering
 Last.fm scrobbling
 Optional Spotify integration for catalog browsing
 Multi-user support
 Cons: 
 No Subsonic API — no third-party mobile apps
 Mobile experience is web-only (responsive, but no native app)
 Requires PHP and MariaDB — heavier stack than Go-based alternatives
 Smaller community than Navidrome or Jellyfin
 No podcast or video support
 APP_KEY must be pre-generated before first start
 Best for: Users who listen primarily from a browser and want the most visually appealing experience. Not ideal if mobile apps matter to you.
 Read our full guide: How to Self-Host Koel 
 5. Ampache -- Most Feature-Rich Legacy Option
 Ampache has been around since 2001, making it one of the oldest self-hosted music servers still actively maintained. That longevity shows — it has an enormous feature set covering music, video, podcasts, radio streams, and Subsonic API compatibility. It supports multiple music catalogs, granular user permissions, and flexible access controls.
 Ampache v7.x modernized the web UI significantly, but it still carries the weight of two decades of features. The PHP/MySQL stack is familiar but heavier than newer Go-based alternatives. If you need features like per-catalog permissions, democratic playback (users vote on the next song), or built-in video support alongside music, Ampache is the only option that does it all.
 Pros: 
 Subsonic API compatible — works with Subsonic mobile apps
 20+ years of feature accumulation — covers edge cases others do not
 Podcast and radio stream support
 Video support alongside music
 Multiple music catalogs with per-catalog permissions
 Democratic playback mode
 Active development (v7.9.2 as of March 2026)
 Cons: 
 UI shows its age despite modernization efforts
 PHP/MySQL stack is heavier to maintain than Go-based servers
 Configuration can be complex due to the sheer number of options
 Documentation is extensive but sometimes outdated
 Scanning large libraries can be slow
 Best for: Power users who need granular control, multiple catalogs, or the combination of music, video, and podcast support in a single server.
 Read our full guide: How to Self-Host Ampache 
 6. gonic -- Lightest Subsonic Server
 gonic strips the concept of a music server down to its essentials. It is a Subsonic-compatible server written in Go with almost no web UI — you manage and listen to your library entirely through Subsonic client apps. This makes it the lightest option available, running on less than 20 MB of RAM.
 gonic supports on-the-fly transcoding, multi-user accounts, Last.fm/ListenBrainz scrobbling, and podcast downloads. It scans your music directory and serves it over the Subsonic API. That is all it does, and it does it well.
 Pros: 
 Extremely lightweight — under 20 MB RAM
 Full Subsonic API compatibility
 Podcast support
 Last.fm and ListenBrainz scrobbling
 Minimal attack surface — barely any web UI to exploit
 Cons: 
 No web UI for playback — you must use Subsonic client apps
 No smart playlists
 No lyrics display
 Smaller community than Navidrome
 Fewer configuration options
 Best for: Users who exclusively use Subsonic mobile apps and want the lightest possible server footprint. Ideal for Raspberry Pi or low-power NAS devices.
 7. Airsonic-Advanced -- Legacy Subsonic Fork
 Airsonic-Advanced is a fork of the original Airsonic project, which itself forked from Subsonic when Subsonic went proprietary. It is a Java application with a web UI, Subsonic API compatibility, podcast support, and jukebox mode.
 Development has slowed significantly. The project's last major release was in 2023, and activity on GitHub is sparse. Navidrome has effectively replaced it in the self-hosted music ecosystem. We include it here for completeness and for users who have existing Airsonic installations.
 Pros: 
 Subsonic API compatible
 Podcast support
 Jukebox mode (play through server speakers)
 Familiar to long-time Subsonic users
 Cons: 
 Development is stalled — last significant release was 2023
 Java-based with higher resource usage (500 MB+ RAM)
 UI feels dated
 Navidrome does everything Airsonic does, but lighter and actively maintained
 Best for: Existing Airsonic users who have not yet migrated. For new installations, use Navidrome instead.
 8. LMS (Logitech Media Server) -- Best for Squeezebox
 LMS is the server component of the Squeezebox ecosystem. If you have Squeezebox hardware or use software Squeezebox players (like piCorePlayer on a Raspberry Pi), LMS is the only real option. It has a massive plugin ecosystem covering internet radio, streaming service integration, multi-room audio, and advanced DSP.
 LMS is a niche pick. It excels in the Squeezebox world but is not a general-purpose music streaming server. If you do not have Squeezebox hardware or software players, skip it.
 Pros: 
 Native Squeezebox ecosystem support
 Enormous plugin library
 Multi-room synchronized audio
 Internet radio integration
 Material Design web interface via plugin
 Cons: 
 Tied to the Squeezebox ecosystem
 Perl-based — unusual stack to maintain
 No Subsonic API
 UI requires a plugin to look modern
 Not a general-purpose music server
 Best for: Squeezebox hardware owners. No one else.
 Honorable Mention: Beets
 Beets is not a streaming server — it is a music library management tool. It fixes tags, fetches metadata from MusicBrainz, normalizes album art, detects duplicates, and organizes files into a consistent directory structure. If your music library is a mess of inconsistent tags and folder names, run Beets before pointing any server at it. Navidrome, Ampache, and every other server on this list will produce better results when fed a well-organized library.
